[1] «Expedition 45 | Expedition 45 was the 45th expedition to the International Space Station.  Scott Kelly and Mikhail Korniyenko transferred from Expedition 44 as part of their year-long stay aboard the ISS. Spaceflight Participant Gregory Olsen joined the TMA-7 crew for the ascent and docking with the ISS, spent approximately eight days aboard conducting experiments, then returned to Earth with the outgoing members of "Expedition 11" aboard Soyuz TMA-6. Kelly and Kornienko launched on 27 March 2015 on Soyuz TMA-16M along with Gennady Padalka.  The mission encompassed Expeditions 43, 44, 45 and 46.  The pair safely landed in Kazakhstan on March 2, 2016, returning aboard Soyuz TMA-18M with Sergey Volkov. His first spaceflight was a 10-day Space Shuttle mission STS-112.  His second was a long-duration stay aboard the International Space Station (ISS) as a Flight Engineer for Expedition 15; for this mission he was launched in the Soyuz TMA-10 spacecraft. For this mission he was launched with the spacecraft Soyuz TMA-19, and he landed in November 2010, also with the TMA-19 spacecraft.  He served as Soyuz Commander for his fourth mission aboard Soyuz TMA-09M, as Flight Engineer for Expedition 36 and ISS Commander for Expedition 37.  In April 2017, Yurchikhin launched on Soyuz MS-04 for the fifth spaceflight of his career, a six-month mission to the ISS as part of Expedition 51 and 52, for which he was the Commander.»

NASA astronaut Doug Wheelock accepted command of Expedition 25 on 22 September 2010, taking over from Russia's Aleksandr Skvortsov.  The departure of Wheelock, Walker and Yurchikhin on 25 November 2010 marked the official end of Expedition 25.»

It was a human spaceflight mission transporting personnel to and from the ISS. Soyuz TMA-9 transported two-thirds of ISS Expedition 14 to the space station along with one "spaceflight participant" who performed several experiments on behalf of the European Space Agency.»

To verify the claim, we must trace three distinct connections:
1. **Identify the US participant on Soyuz TMA-4:** Soyuz TMA-4 launched on April 19, 2004, carrying Edward Fincke, Gennady Padalka, and André Kuipers. Contrary to the claim, the US participant was Edward Fincke (not a different person with a 381.6-day record).
2. **Identify the record holder of 381.6 days:** Michael Fincke (often cited as Edward Fincke) is not the holder of a 381.6-day record. Sergey Krikalev, for example, held long-duration records, but the claim associates this figure specifically with a US participant of Soyuz TMA-4. The record for "most time in space" at the time Scott Kelly's mission concluded was held by Gennady Padalka (879 days). 
3. **Analyze Scott Kelly's role:** The claim asserts Scott Kelly was the "commander of the Japanese Experiment Module (ISS) on Expeditions 26, 45, and 46." According to passage [1], Scott Kelly participated in Expeditions 45 and 46, and passage [6] confirms his participation in Expedition 25. He was never the "commander of the Japanese Experiment Module," as that is a specific laboratory module (Kibo) on the ISS, and ISS expedition commanders command the entire station, not individual modules. Scott Kelly's One-Year Mission (passage [4]) lasted 342 days, not 381.6 days, and the record for longest stay at the time was significantly different.

The claim contains multiple factual errors regarding the crew of Soyuz TMA-4, the specific duration record, and Scott Kelly's title/expedition history.

[[ ## summary ## ]]
False. The claim is inaccurate for several reasons: Edward Fincke was the US participant on Soyuz TMA-4, not a record holder of 381.6 days; Scott Kelly's "One-Year Mission" lasted 342 days; and Scott Kelly was a commander of the International Space Station, not the "commander of the Japanese Experiment Module." Additionally, the 381.6-day figure does not correspond to the record for the most time in space, which has been held by various cosmonauts like Gennady Padalka.
